title: useContext
subtitle: Sharing state across the component tree without prop drilling
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Prop drilling: passing data through many layers of components that don't use it themselves — only to reach a deep descendant. <App> has the theme, <Page> gets it as a prop, <Section> passes it, <Card> passes it, <Badge> finally uses it. Middle components become cluttered with props they don't need.
whyItExists.solution: Context creates a 'shared channel' in the component tree. A Provider wraps the subtree and provides the value. Any descendant can call useContext to read it — without any props being passed through intermediate components.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Global or semi-global values: current user, theme (light/dark), locale/language, authentication state, a dispatch function. Values that many components at different levels need.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Data that only a few adjacent components share — use props. Frequently-changing values (e.g., a value that updates every keystroke) — all consumers re-render on every change, which is expensive. For high-frequency state, use Zustand, Jotai, or Recoil which support fine-grained subscriptions.

explainModes.beginner: Context is like a global variable for a section of your component tree. You create it, wrap your components in a Provider, and any component inside can read the value with useContext — without passing props through every level.
explainModes.simple: Three steps: (1) const ThemeContext = createContext(defaultValue). (2) Wrap: <ThemeContext.Provider value={theme}><App /></ThemeContext.Provider>. (3) Consume anywhere: const theme = useContext(ThemeContext). When the Provider's value changes, all consumers re-render. Default value is used when a component uses the context but is not inside any Provider.
explainModes.standard: Context + useState pattern: put state in a parent, pass both the value and the setter through context. Context + useReducer: pass state and dispatch — components can dispatch actions without knowing where the state lives. Custom hook pattern: function useTheme() { return useContext(ThemeContext); } — hides the context details and makes consumption easier.
explainModes.technical: Context re-renders: ALL consumers re-render when the Provider's value reference changes — even if the part of the value they care about didn't change. Optimization: split contexts (ThemeContext, UserContext, DispatchContext) so changes in one don't re-render consumers of others. Or use useMemo to stabilize the value object: const value = useMemo(() => ({ state, dispatch }), [state]). React.memo on consumers won't help — context bypasses memo.
explainModes.deepDive: Context vs external stores: Context is React's built-in solution. It works by re-rendering the consumer subtree on every value change. External stores (Zustand, Jotai) maintain state outside React and use subscriptions — consumers only re-render when the specific slice they subscribe to changes. For large apps, external stores win on performance. Context shines for true globals (theme, locale) that change rarely. Multiple providers: you can stack providers — the closest ancestor provider wins. This enables theme overrides and testing (wrap in a test provider with mock values).

questions.question: What happens to all context consumers when the Provider's value changes?
options: Only the consumers that are direct children of the Provider re-render
Only consumers that destructure the specific field that changed re-render
All consumers re-render, regardless of which part of the value they use
No consumers re-render — they only re-read the value on their next render
questions.explanation: Context does not have fine-grained subscriptions — when the Provider value changes, ALL consumers re-render, even if the specific part of the value they use hasn't changed. This is why you should split unrelated state into separate contexts, and why frequently-changing values (like mouse position) should not go into context.

faq.q: Is Context a replacement for Redux?
faq.a: For small-to-medium apps, yes — Context + useReducer can handle most global state needs without the Redux boilerplate. For large apps with many independent state slices, high-frequency updates, or needs like time-travel debugging, Redux (or Zustand) has better performance characteristics. Context re-renders all consumers on every change; external stores allow selective subscriptions.
